name: Hari Singh Nalwa
role: Commander-in-chief of the Sikh Khalsa Army under Maharaja Ranjit Singh
summary: The famous commander and governor who guarded the Khyber frontier for Maharaja Ranjit Singh, remembered for the tiger-killing tale and for the forts he built.
about: Hari Singh Nalwa was born in 1791 in Gujranwala and joined the court of Maharaja Ranjit Singh as a boy. Sikh and Punjabi tradition says he killed a tiger on a hunting trip, earning the nickname Baghmar. He fought at Kasur, Sialkot, Multan, Attock, Nowshera and Peshawar, and took Jamrud at the mouth of the Khyber Pass in 1836. He also governed Kashmir, Hazara and Peshawar and founded the town of Haripur. Sikh rule in Kashmir, which he governed in 1820-21, is generally described as oppressive. Accounts differ on the exact origin of the name Nalwa and on how he died in 1837 at Jamrud. Afghan folk stories say mothers invoked his name to quiet children, though this story is reported in later Sikh sources rather than documents. He is remembered in Punjab as a symbol of bravery and strong frontier defence.
kidSummary: Hari Singh Nalwa was a famous Sikh general who served Maharaja Ranjit Singh. A popular story says he fought off a tiger on a hunt, and people called him Baghmar. He built forts and a town named Haripur and guarded the Khyber Pass.

story.title: A boy at the court
story.text: Hari Singh was born in Gujranwala in 1791. In 1804 he went to Maharaja Ranjit Singh's court and was made an attendant.

story.title: The tiger on the hunt
story.text: The story goes that a tiger attacked him during a hunt. He refused help and fought it himself with a dagger and shield.

story.title: A name is born
story.text: People began to call him Baghmar, meaning tiger-killer. The Maharaja trusted him and gave him a command of 800 soldiers.

story.title: Commander and builder
story.text: He fought at Kasur, Multan, Attock and Peshawar. He also built forts and founded the town of Haripur in 1822.

story.title: Guard of the Khyber
story.text: In 1836 he took Jamrud near the Khyber Pass. He died there in 1837, and Sikhs and Punjabis still tell stories about him.

emblems: Dagger and shield (in the tiger story)
texts: Court histories of the Sikh Empire

facts.text: India's first individual Olympic gold medallist, shooter Abhinav Bindra, is a fifth-generation direct descendant of Hari Singh Nalwa.

According to the usual story, a tiger attacked him on a hunt in 1804 and killed his horse. He refused help and is said to have killed it himself with a dagger and shield, earning the name Baghmar, meaning tiger-killer.
Multan was attacked seven times in Ranjit Singh's time and he fought in five; in 1810 he was badly wounded by a fire-pot thrown during the assault.
He died on 30 April 1837 at Jamrud. Accounts disagree on how: an Afghan chronicle says he fell in a duel with Wazir Akbar Khan, while another account says two bullets struck him as he led his men.

His lieutenant Mahan Singh is said to have kept his death secret until reinforcements reached the fort. Wikipedia adds that the Afghans knew he was wounded but waited over a week before it was confirmed, and left after seeing his body hung outside the fort.
Wikipedia reports that Afghan mothers used his name to scare crying children, saying that Haria Ragle, meaning Hari Singh Nalwa, would come.

The Tribune says Ranjit Singh was impressed by the tiger story and cried out praise comparing him to Nal, the legendary hero of the Mahabharata. That praise is said to have grown into the name Nalwa, though accounts of the name differ.
Ranjit Singh enjoyed hearing about victories over the Afghans so much that he ordered a Kashmir shawl, at the record price of 5,000 rupees, showing scenes from those battles.
In September 2023 a depiction of him appeared on official sweater merchandise of the Dallas Cowboys American football team, as part of a theme called Carpe Omnia.
He was also a religious builder. He built Gurdwara Panja Sahib at Hassan Abdal to mark Guru Nanak's journey, and donated the gold used to cover the dome of the Akal Takht at Amritsar.
At least 56 buildings are credited to him, including forts, towers, gurdwaras, temples, mosques, tanks, towns, sarais and gardens.
He set up a mint to help collect revenue in Kashmir and Peshawar, and the Tribune says he introduced the HariSinghee coin in Kashmir for tax collection.

Wikipedia says that during his governorship in Kashmir (1820-21), Sikh rule there was generally considered oppressive. Laws included death for cow slaughter, the closing of Srinagar's Jamia Masjid and a ban on the public call to prayer.

In the Michni account, he went hunting with 100 horsemen and then attacked a local khan's house at night after Hindu villagers complained that the khan had taken a man's wife. Accounts differ on how the khan met his end.
He did not always win. In December 1834 Akbar Khan, son of Dost Mohammad Khan, beat him in a skirmish, leaving about 150 Sikhs dead or wounded and forcing him back to Peshawar.
When the Afghans advanced on Jamrud in 1837, his lieutenant Mahan Singh held the small fort with about 600 men, short of supplies and water. Hari Singh rode out from Peshawar to relieve them.

In 1831 he led a diplomatic mission to the British Governor-General Lord William Bentinck. Before the Ropar meeting he spoke strongly against the plan to have the British accept Kharak Singh as Ranjit Singh's heir.
In the 1818 siege of Multan, which the Sikhs took on the sixth attempt, Wikipedia calls him chiefly instrumental in capturing the citadel. The famous Zamzama cannon was badly damaged in that siege.

In the 1827 battle against Sayyid Ahmad's force near Attock, one side shouted Allah hu Akbar and the other answered Sat Sri Akal. Wikipedia notes that both were praising the same God in different languages.
Amar Chitra Katha first published his biography in 1978, and a commemorative postage stamp honouring him was released on 30 April 2013, the 176th anniversary of his death.
His town of Haripur had a superb water distribution system. When the traveller Hügel visited in 1835-36 he found it busy, and many Khatri families had settled there to trade.

quiz.q: Which town did he found in 1822?
At which fort did he die?
At the mouth of which pass did he capture a fort in 1836?
quiz.why: Jamrud is at the mouth of the Khyber Pass.
